text: The 'location problem' that arises for the deprivation account of death's badness is the difficulty of specifying:
choices: why death is bad, given that the person who has died undergoes no bad experiences.
whether the statement that there will be a sea battle tomorrow is true today.
which particular future people are made worse off by a resource-depleting policy.
when, and for whom, death is bad, given that after death there is no subject who exists to be harmed.
explanation: The location problem asks at what time, and to which subject, the harm of death attaches: none of the ante-mortem, moment-of-death, or post-mortem options is fully satisfactory, since after death no subject exists to bear the harm. Option A states what the deprivation account explains (why death is bad), not the timing puzzle. The sea-battle truth-value question belongs to logical fatalism, and the worry about which future people are harmed is Parfit's non-identity problem, both drawn from elsewhere in the unit.
